Summary: New Statista research and expert insight on what it takes to build real-world supply chain flexibility. When was the last time your logistics plan actually went to plan? In logistics, disruption is expected. But while many operators are taking the opportunity posed by more route options and modes through Southeast Asia, new research suggests that the logistics systems aren’t keeping up.

**More options, more routes, but not more resilience**
 Last year, trade between China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) exceeded US$1.05 trillion. Manufacturing hubs are spreading across the region, requiring more freight options, all of this against a backdrop of almost constant disruption. Each shift forces companies to rethink how – and sometimes where – they move inventory.

87% of logistics decision-makers in the area say they’ve responded by increasing their use of multimodal routes. However, 92% describe diversified routing as only partially implemented across their networks.

Across four separate measures in our research, just 0-2% of respondents selected the highest level of routing implementation, partner connectivity, public-authority integration, or end-to-end visibility.

Diversifying route options is only the first step. There must also be capacity available. Commercial arrangements need to be ready. The handovers need to work. And someone needs to have the authority to make the call. Without those elements, a path that looks like resilience on paper can offer little flexibility when a disruption actually happens.

> Ever since COVID, there is that vast volatility in the supply chain…every year we will have some disruption.’’
> _Kevin Burrell, Maersk – Managing Director – Mekong_

[![Image 2](https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/08796.jpg)](https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/08796.jpg)

**Knee-jerk responses to disruption**
 Over the past 12-24 months, 69% of the logistics leaders say chokepoints have affected their operations significantly or very significantly. Most are reacting to each crisis, rather than planning for them – increasing safety stock by 50% or turning to last-minute airfreight options. In both cases, operators are paying more to live with an unpredictable network.

Discover more

Shipping news subscription

Daily shipping news

Freight transport services

**The real resilience builder: systems, data, partners and handovers that make full use of the route options**
 Transporting freight from China through Southeast Asia can involve a long chain of organisations: freight forwarders, trucking companies, terminals, customs agencies, brokers, ports, airlines, shipping lines and warehouses might all touch the same shipment.

Individually, many of those organisations are well equipped, but each handover creates a black hole of information – and every additional mode creates another handover.

So, while additional modes and gateways give you more ways around a disruption, they also give you more points where information – and accountability – disappear. Those weak points are also inconsistent across regions – research found high lead-time variability across both respondent groups, but with different problems underneath. This shows why the same solution can’t simply be applied to every corridor.

Lack of digitisation isn’t the issue, either – 91% of organisations already use digital documentation, for example, but 51% also report limited integration with external partners.

**The solution: stop looking for the perfect route**
 The strongest logistics networks can recognise when current routes won’t work, identify the right alternative, and activate it quickly. For most organisations, that doesn’t mean rebuilding the entire network at once. Instead, you need to:

[![Image 3](https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/8756-1.jpg)](https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/8756-1.jpg)

[![Image 4](https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/09090909.jpg)](https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/09090909.jpg)

**The ideal route exists – it just changes every day**
 Successful players will have a network agile enough to find and execute it.

Discover more

Online newspaper access

Track Sea Cargo

Read Daily News

No route or strategy is an ideal fit for the China-Southeast Asia corridor. What works is increasing the maturity of your network and processes to buffer selectively, diversify deliberately, and prepare your response to disruption.

**How resilient is your supply chain?**
 Research conducted with 260 logistics and supply chain decision-makers across Asia-Pacific found that organisations differ significantly in their ability to anticipate, absorb and respond to disruption.

To help organisations evaluate their readiness, No Perfect Route introduces a Supply Chain Resilience Maturity Model that identifies five stages of resilience capability, from reactive response to proactive orchestration.

Most organisations operate somewhere within this spectrum.

Understanding where you sit is the first step towards improvement.

**MATURITY MODEL – what stage are you?**
 Most organisations can be placed in one of five stages of maturity. Understanding where yours sits is an important starting point for improving resilience.

**Stage 1: Reactive**
 You handle disruptions through ad hoc, manual firefighting after cargo is already delayed. Fallback corridors are mostly on paper.

**Stage 2: Managed**
 Basic visibility tools exist, but modal shifts remain manual, siloed, and heavily dependent on tribal knowledge and key individuals. This leaves your network vulnerable when key staff are unavailable.

**Stage 3: Connected**
 Systems exchange data across supply chain partners, but execution relies on checkpoint updates rather than real-time tracking. You still absorb delays because your teams only discover disruptions after the fact.

**Stage 4: Orchestrated**
 Alternative routes are pre-costed, pre-tested, and backed by pre-approved decision rights. Your team switches modes rapidly, protecting the bottom line and safeguarding customer delivery dates.

**Stage 5: Proactive**
 Predictive external signals (weather, port congestion, tariffs) are integrated into live routing, adjusting flows before disruption impacts customer delivery.
 Source: Maersk

title: US Defence Intelligence warns of expanding Chinese and Russian counterspace threats
summary: [![Image 1](https://spaceanddefense.io/wp-content/smush-webp/2026/10/DIA.jpg.webp)](https://spaceanddefense.io/wp-content/smush-webp/2026/10/DIA.jpg.webp) The United States Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) has released a new assessment of
content:
[![Image 1](https://spaceanddefense.io/wp-content/smush-webp/2026/10/DIA.jpg.webp)](https://spaceanddefense.io/wp-content/smush-webp/2026/10/DIA.jpg.webp)

The United States Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) has released a new assessment of global space security, warning that China and Russia are expanding their military and dual-use space capabilities as competition intensifies over access to and control of Earth’s orbital environment.

The third edition of [Challenges to Security in Space](https://www.dia.mil/Portals/110/Images/News/Military_Powers_Publications/Challenges_Security_Space_2026.pdf) examines the military space strategies, capabilities and intentions of China and Russia, alongside the emerging space programs of Iran and North Korea.

The unclassified assessment identifies the expansion of counterspace capabilities, growing cooperation between US strategic competitors and increasing dependence on commercial satellite infrastructure as significant challenges to international security.

The DIA says the report is intended to improve public understanding of the threats to US national security and the extent to which space is increasingly treated as a warfighting domain. Its intelligence assessment is current to July 2026.

**China and Russia expand counterspace capabilities**

The report identifies China and Russia as the principal countries developing capabilities intended to challenge US and allied space operations.

According to the assessment, both countries are pursuing technologies capable of disrupting, degrading or destroying satellites and the services they provide. These include electronic warfare, cyber operations, directed-energy systems and kinetic anti-satellite weapons.

China’s military space development is particularly significant because of its expanding satellite fleets, surveillance capabilities and investments in technologies that could support both civilian and military missions.

The DIA assessment indicates that China may develop space-based directed-energy capabilities capable of threatening satellites in higher orbits by the late 2020s. This is a projection rather than confirmation that such weapons have been deployed.

Russia continues to pursue counterspace capabilities, including electronic warfare and anti-satellite systems, while seeking to maintain its military space capabilities despite the financial and technological pressures associated with the war in Ukraine.

The assessment also raises concerns about Russia’s development of potentially nuclear-armed anti-satellite capabilities, an issue previously identified by the US intelligence community.

**Ukraine conflict demonstrates the military importance of commercial satellites**

The war in Ukraine has provided a significant demonstration of how commercial space systems can influence military operations.

Commercial satellite communications, Earth observation and geospatial intelligence have supported Ukrainian battlefield awareness, military coordination and operational resilience.

The DIA identifies Russia’s efforts to disrupt commercial satellite services supporting Ukraine, including through electronic jamming, as evidence of the growing vulnerability of privately operated space infrastructure during armed conflict.

Russia has also publicly characterised certain commercial satellite systems supporting Ukrainian military operations as potential military targets.

The report highlights the strategic implications of this development as governments increasingly rely on commercial providers for communications, intelligence collection and other defence-related services.

The growing integration of commercial satellite constellations into military operations is also creating new questions about infrastructure protection, service continuity and the responsibilities of private operators during conflict.

**Growing cooperation between strategic competitors**

The assessment also examines increasing cooperation between China, Russia, Iran and North Korea in space-related activities.

The DIA identifies Chinese support for Russian space capabilities, including the provision of components and technology, as part of a broader pattern of cooperation between the two countries.

China and Russia are also expanding international partnerships involving satellite services, launch capabilities and space technology development.

The agency assesses that these relationships can strengthen military capabilities while extending diplomatic and economic influence.

Both countries are increasingly integrating commercial, academic and civilian space expertise into national security programs, further blurring the distinction between civilian and military space activities.

The report identifies Iran and North Korea as emerging space powers whose capabilities and international relationships warrant continued monitoring.

**Cybersecurity and electronic warfare emerge as major vulnerabilities**

The increasing integration of satellites into terrestrial communications, navigation, intelligence and critical infrastructure systems is creating additional opportunities for cyber and electronic attacks.

Unlike destructive anti-satellite weapons, cyber intrusions and electronic warfare can potentially disrupt satellite services without generating orbital debris.

These methods can interfere with communications, compromise information integrity or temporarily deny access to positioning, navigation and timing services.

The US intelligence community has previously warned that attacks against space-enabled services are becoming more common and that vulnerabilities associated with satellite communications are expanding as digital networks become increasingly interconnected.

These developments place greater importance on protecting ground stations, satellite control networks, communications links and the supply chains supporting space operations.

**Orbital congestion adds to security concerns**

Beyond deliberate threats, the DIA examines the increasing congestion of Earth’s orbital environment and the hazards created by space debris.

The rapid expansion of satellite constellations, combined with debris generated by previous anti-satellite tests, is increasing the complexity of maintaining safe and sustainable space operations.

Destructive anti-satellite weapons can create debris that remains in orbit for extended periods, potentially threatening satellites operated by countries not involved in a conflict.

The Secure World Foundation’s 2026 assessment of global counterspace capabilities identified 6,904 catalogued debris objects generated by anti-satellite testing conducted by the United States, Russia, China and India, of which 2,773 remained in orbit at the time of its analysis.

The figures illustrate the enduring consequences of destructive counterspace activity and the importance of space domain awareness, collision avoidance and international coordination.

**Implications for Australia and Indo-Pacific space security**

The DIA assessment has particular relevance to Australia and its Indo-Pacific security partnerships, where satellite communications, Earth observation and positioning services are increasingly important to defence operations and economic infrastructure.

Australia’s geographic position, ground station infrastructure and expanding commercial space industry make the resilience of space-enabled services an important national security consideration.

The report’s findings reinforce the strategic significance of space domain awareness, assured satellite communications, cybersecurity and the ability to maintain critical services during disruption.

They also highlight the importance of understanding the dependencies between military operations and commercial satellite networks, particularly where essential capabilities are provided by private companies or international partners.

For Australia’s emerging sovereign space industry, the changing threat environment presents challenges extending beyond spacecraft manufacturing and launch. Secure ground infrastructure, resilient communications architectures, protected supply chains and trusted international partnerships are increasingly important elements of operational capability.

The broader significance of the DIA report is its assessment that space security can no longer be considered separately from terrestrial military operations, economic infrastructure and geopolitical competition.

As commercial and military space activities continue to expand, maintaining reliable access to orbit and protecting satellite-enabled services will become increasingly important to governments, defence organisations and commercial operators throughout the Indo-Pacific.

The report also underscores a central strategic challenge: the same technologies making space more accessible and economically valuable are increasing the number of systems potentially exposed to interference, attack and conflict.

title: Building a China-resilient battery chain by 2035 – GIS Reports
summary: The West can loosen China’s hold without fully decoupling by developing alternative supply sources. Processing plants and settling tanks at Zijin Mining’s Xiangyuan lithium mine in Hunan province, built to process 5 million tons of ore a ye
content:
The West can loosen China’s hold without fully decoupling by developing alternative supply sources.

Processing plants and settling tanks at Zijin Mining’s Xiangyuan lithium mine in Hunan province, built to process 5 million tons of ore a year. China’s real leverage lies in what happens after extraction: turning ore into battery-grade materials. © Getty Images

GIS Radio

0:00 / 20:57

Listen to our AI-powered podcast for comprehensive insights.

[Audio 3](https://www.gisreportsonline.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Building-a-China-resilient-battery-supply-chain-by-2035.mp3)

*   China’s grip on processing makes a full break too expensive
*   The West can cut its dependence on China, not eliminate it
*   New battery technologies will ease the dependence, not end it

_This report is the next installment in a series on_[_mineral diplomacy_](https://www.gisreportsonline.com/t/mineral-diplomacy/)_from GIS expert Bob Savic_.

Western battery and electric-vehicle (EV) supply chains remain heavily dependent on China, and Beijing has shown it is willing to use that leverage. A fully China-free supply chain by 2035 is unlikely, and pursuing one would be prohibitively expensive and technologically disruptive. A far less China-dependent system, however, is achievable. The realistic goal is “selective de-risking”: cutting exposure in refining, cathodes, graphite and magnets far enough that a Chinese cutoff becomes a disruption rather than a shutdown.

On current trajectories, the West and its allies may build credible alternatives for lithium-ion cell assembly and some upstream inputs by 2035. Even so, China is likely to remain the cheapest and most dominant supplier of refined materials, cathodes, anodes and magnets.

[![Image 2](https://www.gisreportsonline.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/advisory-1.png)](https://gisadvisory.com/)
## Scale of the dependence

The International Energy Agency (IEA) identifies China as the leading refiner for [19 of 20 strategic minerals](https://www.iea.org/commentaries/with-new-export-controls-on-critical-minerals-supply-concentration-risks-become-reality), with an average share of approximately 70 percent. In [magnet rare earths](https://www.iea.org/reports/rare-earth-elements/executive-summary), China accounted for around 60 percent of global mining in 2024 but approximately 91 percent of refining. The imbalance is even more pronounced in permanent magnets: Outside China, planned magnet capacity by 2035 amounts to only about one-third of expected mine output, and current and announced projects would meet less than one-fifth of non-Chinese magnet demand.

These dependencies have already been tested. The IEA reports that China’s 2025 export controls on medium and heavy rare earths and related products sharply reduced exports and forced some European and North American automakers to cut or temporarily suspend production.

Beijing’s advantage is not primarily geological. It lies in the midstream and downstream stages that turn ore into usable products – chemical conversion, separation and manufacturing cathodes and anodes. Owning these processes also means owning the know-how, equipment and integrated industrial ecosystems that support them. Opening a mine outside China does not automatically create a secure supply chain if the concentrate is still shipped to China for refining, or if Chinese technology converts the refined material into cathodes.

This creates three distinct vulnerabilities. First, the West may secure mineral resources but lack sufficient refining capacity. Second, it may build cell factories that still rely on Chinese imported components, equipment or process licenses.Third, it may diversify suppliers on paper while those suppliers retain Chinese ownership, technology or feedstock links. A supply chain can therefore appear geographically diversified while remaining politically concentrated.

### Share of refined material production by country in 2025 vs. the top producer’s share in 2023

## Refining is the critical bottleneck

Reducing dependence on Chinese refining is feasible, but it is the hardest and most capital-intensive step to replicate. Mines are slow to develop: New projects can sometimes come online within a decade, though permitting disputes and local opposition often extend that timeline.

Refining is less politically contentious but more technically demanding. It requires specialized chemical processes, reliable energy and water, hazardous-waste management, skilled labor and long-term offtake agreements to justify the investment.

The [IEA’s 2035 outlook](https://www.iea.org/reports/global-critical-minerals-outlook-2026) is sobering. Even if every planned project is completed on schedule, Beijing’s share is projected to decline at most to 70 percent by 2035. Under current-policy assumptions, China is expected to retain more than 60 percent of refined lithium and cobalt, while its share of battery-grade graphite and magnet rare earths is likely to remain close to 80 percent.

The cost of changing this trajectory is substantial. IEA estimates suggest that meeting non-Chinese demand for magnet rare earths could require roughly $60 billion in investment over the next decade. A comprehensive Western program covering battery materials, magnets and associated equipment would likely require public subsidies and guarantees well beyond the headline cost of individual projects.

The economic challenge is that Chinese facilities benefit from scale, integrated supply chains, lower capital costs and a mature supplier ecosystem. Non-Chinese projects may therefore be commercially uncompetitive during periods of low prices. Governments will need to compensate through concessional finance and binding procurement commitments. Without these mechanisms, private investors may build capacity only when prices spike – precisely when construction is most expensive and supply is most constrained.

## Coalition-building

No individual Western country can economically recreate the entire battery supply chain. A functioning alternative would require a coalition in which each member contributes what it does best.

The United States combines financial power with a vast automotive and energy-storage market, while defense demand and tax incentives let it guarantee buyers for new capacity. Canada and Australia offer what the coalition most lacks outside China: mines and the processing expertise to go with them, in politically reliable hands. The United Kingdom could contribute financial services, magnets and recycling capabilities.

The European Union’s main asset is regulatory leverage over one of the world’s largest automotive markets, supported by deep chemical-engineering expertise. Japan’s main contribution is experience: decades spent reducing its dependence on rare earths, backed by state resource finance. South Korea contributes battery manufacturing, cathode technology and global industrial networks.

Japan-U.S. cooperation already illustrates the required model. The two countries’ October 2025 [critical minerals framework](https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefings-statements/2025/10/united-states-japan-framework-for-securing-the-supply-of-critical-minerals-and-rare-earths-through-mining-and-processing/) goes well beyond extraction, covering separation and processing, project finance, permitting, scrap management and stockpiling, and a joint rapid-response group for supply disruptions. Cooperation with South Korea could extend this into a trilateral division of labor, linking Korean battery manufacturers with Japanese materials expertise and North American mineral and processing projects.

Extending the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing arrangement – comprising the U.S., UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand – to critical minerals could support early-warning systems and coordinated investment screening. However, the Five Eyes countries lack the industrial capacity to offset China’s dominance.

The [EU’s Critical Raw Materials Act](https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/sectors/raw-materials/areas-specific-interest/critical-raw-materials/critical-raw-materials-act_en) provides a useful policy architecture. Its 2030 benchmarks call for 10 percent of annual strategic-material consumption from domestic extraction, 40 percent from domestic processing, 25 percent from recycling and no more than 65 percent from any single third country. However, Europe cannot economically mine and process every input domestically. Its more realistic role is to build selected strategic capabilities while securing diversified supply from allied and resource-rich partners.

Coalition-building will still face political friction. The U.S. may favor domestic production and protectionist subsidies; the EU may prioritize open trade and regulatory standards; Japan and South Korea will seek reliable access without being compelled to fully align with Washington; and resource-rich developing states will resist arrangements that perpetuate a purely extractive relationship.

A durable coalition should offer partner countries investment, skills and infrastructure; a stake in local processing; and a transparent share of the revenue that comes with it – not simply requests for guaranteed mineral exports.

April 6, 2026: Mountain Pass in California, America’s only active rare earth mine, is central to Washington’s push to build a magnet supply chain outside China. © Getty Images

## Beijing’s retaliation risk

In response to Western efforts to rebuild their battery supply chains, China has several options short of a comprehensive embargo. Its most effective tools are administrative rather than dramatic: tighter export licensing, broader definitions of dual-use goods and quiet pressure on Chinese firms to limit dealings with Western partners. It can also mandate higher domestic inventories or use price competition to bankrupt non-Chinese projects.

China’s 2025 export controls, which targeted everything from rare earth products to graphite anode materials and battery equipment, showed how Beijing can hit multiple points simultaneously. Retaliation would probably be calibrated rather than absolute. A total embargo would accelerate Western substitution, damage Chinese exporters and encourage permanent stockpiling.

Controls can also be applied selectively. For example, Beijing could permit civilian battery exports while restricting high-performance magnets, defense-related materials, production equipment or products containing Chinese-origin inputs.

The greatest vulnerability is not a single shipment interruption but a legal and commercial “rules-of-origin” issue. If China asserts controls over foreign-made products that contain Chinese materials or are manufactured using Chinese technology, assembly in Europe or North America will not guarantee independence.

## Will technology substitution make the contest moot?

Technology substitution will reduce some dependencies, but it is unlikely to render the supply-chain struggle irrelevant by 2035.

Sodium-ion batteries are the most plausible near-term alternative. They reduce or eliminate dependence on lithium, nickel and cobalt, and could be attractive for low-cost vehicles, two- and three-wheelers, grid storage and cold climates. Their disadvantages include lower energy density, limited production scale and a nascent supply chain that is itself concentrated in China.

Solid-state batteries could eventually shift the strategic balance more substantially. They may improve safety and enable higher energy density, while some designs reduce reliance on graphite or alter cathode requirements. The IEA notes that solid-state deployment is likely to remain concentrated in premium vehicle segments during the first half of the 2030s, with early commercial launches expected and larger-scale production planned later in the decade.

content:
### Wang Yi Holds Talks with Foreign Minister of the Republic of the Congo Constant-Serge Bounda

2026-10-22 23:00 Print

* * *

On October 22, 2026, Member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and Foreign Minister Wang Yi held talks with Foreign Minister of the Republic of the Congo Constant-Serge Bounda in Beijing.

Wang Yi stated that President Xi Jinping and President Denis Sassou Nguesso have established solid mutual trust and friendship, which provides an important political guarantee for the development of China-Congo relations, and that bilateral relations enjoy a strong momentum of development. The Republic of the Congo is the first African country to reach an early harvest arrangement with China under the agreement on economic partnership for shared development, and cooperation between the two countries in various fields has yielded positive results. China appreciates the Congolese side's adherence to the one-China principle and its support for China's legitimate position of safeguarding its core interests. China will also continue to support the Congolese side in pursuing a development path suited to its national conditions, keeping the destiny of the country in its own hands, and opposing all forms of bullying by any external forces.

Wang Yi noted that China is ready, under the strategic guidance of the two heads of state, to work with the Congolese side to plan high-level exchanges for the next stage, strengthen strategic alignment, steadily advance practical cooperation, and bring bilateral relations to a new level. China and the Republic of the Congo actively fulfill their responsibilities as co-chairs of the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation (FOCAC), and the implementation rate of the outcomes of the Beijing Summit has approached 100 percent. The two sides should continue to maintain close coordination and prepare for the 10th Ministerial Conference, scheduled to be held in the Republic of the Congo in 2027, to advance a new round of upgrading and improvement of China-Africa cooperation.

Wang Yi stated that the role of the United Nations is currently facing challenges, unilateralism and protectionism are rampant, and the international order has been severely impacted. China supports African countries in playing a greater role on the international stage, and is ready to work with Africa to firmly safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of developing countries, promote the democratization of international relations, and build a more just and equitable global governance system that meets the common aspirations of Global South countries. The Republic of the Congo is a founding state party to the International Organization for Mediation and a founding member of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization. The two sides should make good use of these multilateral platforms, strengthen communication and coordination, and uphold fairness and justice.

Constant-Serge Bounda stated that China is a good friend and good brother of the Republic of the Congo, and the two sides have always trusted and supported each other. The Congolese side is ready to work with China, under the guidance of the two heads of state, to deepen cooperation in various fields and advance the building of a high-level Congo-China community with a shared future. The Congolese side supports the series of global initiatives proposed by President Xi Jinping, and reaffirms its firm adherence to the one-China principle. The current international and regional situation is complex and severe, peace and security are under threat, and it is necessary for the Global South to strengthen solidarity and cooperation. China's zero-tariff policy has broadly benefited African countries, including the Republic of the Congo. The Congolese side appreciates China's emphasis on Africa's health undertakings and its assistance to Africa in combating the Ebola epidemic and strengthening health infrastructure. The Congolese side is ready to work with China to jointly prepare for the new Ministerial Conference of FOCAC and promote new and greater development of Africa-China relations.

title: China Hits Out at Trump’s Golden Dome as U.S. Intel Says Beijing Could Deploy Space-Based Laser Weapons by Late 2020s
summary: **The US Defense Intelligence Agency said in a new assessment that China could deploy space-based directed-energy weapons by the late 2020s, adding to an existing suite of ground-based systems already capable of affecting satellites.** Titl
content:
**The US Defense Intelligence Agency said in a new assessment that China could deploy space-based directed-energy weapons by the late 2020s, adding to an existing suite of ground-based systems already capable of affecting satellites.**

Titled “Challenges to Security in Space,” and published on October 26, the assessment is the third in a series of reports examining the military space programs of China and Russia, as well as emerging capabilities in Iran and North Korea.

Although China already fields an array of ground-based lasers capable of disrupting, degrading, or damaging satellites in low Earth orbit, the DIA report said it could deploy these directed-energy weapons in space and field more powerful ground-based systems that could threaten American satellites by the end of the 2020s.

These DEWs will be part of a broader Chinese counterspace arsenal that includes electronic warfare, cyber tools, kinetic anti-satellite (ASAT) missiles, and co-orbital platforms.

The assessment follows US Space Force Gen. Stephen Whiting’s August 2026 public [assertion](https://www.eurasiantimes.com/america-is-losing-the-space-war-top-u-s-general-demands-weapons-to-outdo-russia-china-in-orbit/) that China has ASAT missiles, ground-based lasers, jammers, and maneuverable, dual-use satellites.

“These developments intend to degrade our current space superiority and would potentially give China a maneuver and logistics advantage in space – something we would not accept on the land, at sea, or in the air,” he emphasized at the time.

Directed-energy weapons, for one, transmit concentrated electromagnetic energy, including high-power lasers or high-power microwaves, toward a target to damage, disable, disrupt, or destroy it, rather than relying primarily on conventional fires, shells, or missiles.

DEWs are significantly cheaper than conventional weapons.

Chinese state-owned media dismissed the reports as “hype,” accusing the United States of raising alarms about purported space threats even as it presses ahead with its own orbital military buildup, deploys weapons in space, and advances the aspirational space-based **Golden Dome missile defense initiative**.

Buy Home Safes

## **US Already Has Weapons in Space**

While the above is typical of a Chinese response to such accusations, the United States has indeed placed weapons in space whilst cautioning about the domain’s militarization.

USAF Secretary Troy Meink said in September 2026 that the country now possesses “on-orbit space control weapons” capable of defending US and allied forces, as the EurAsian Times [reported](https://www.eurasiantimes.com/1967-outer-space-treaty-u-s-admits-weapons-in-space-why-are-china-russia-calling-it-a-violation/) at the time.

Although he did not say which weapons the US has deployed, US Space Force doctrine emphasizes “space control,” the ability to contest and control the space domain using kinetic and/or non-kinetic means to disrupt, degrade, or destroy adversary capabilities. Thus, the deployed weapons can serve either offensive or defensive purposes.

Discover more

Chinese military technology

J-20 fighter models

H-20 stealth bomber

Meink linked the deployment to threats from China and Russia, asking rhetorically whether anyone doubted those countries’ development of similar weapons. “It is critically important that we maintain our dominance not only in the air but in space, and so we’ve had to take steps to make sure that when we’re threatened, we can take care of that,” he asserted.

At the time, the Chinese foreign ministry responded to the U.S. announcement by accusing Washington of “preparing for war in outer space” and warning against turning space into a battlefield or triggering an arms race, the same things it often campaigns against.

When asked whether the admission of placing weapons in space amounts to militarization of space by the US and if it could trigger an arms race, Group Captain Pandey (retd) told the EurAsian Times, “By design, the Pentagon wants potential adversaries to know that an operational defensive and offensive counterspace shield exists in orbit, without revealing how it functions. Disclosing exact specifications (such as frequencies, physical yield, or tracking systems) would allow rivals to develop countermeasures.”

“Meink’s emphasis on innovating faster than competitors highlights the rapid technological race between the US, China, and Russia. Because space capabilities can be upgraded or deployed faster than ground infrastructure, staying ahead depends on continuous deployment, autonomous software, and rapid launch iterations,” he added.

Whether US systems include directed-energy weapons remains unknown and is the subject of speculation. However, non-kinetic options such as electronic warfare or jamming payloads are currently believed to be among the more plausible options for early on-orbit deployments, as they avoid generating debris.

File Image: Chinese Space Station

## **From Ground-Based To Space-Based DEWs**

China already fields a host of directed-energy systems, including counter-drone laser weapons and military-grade dazzlers used to intercept other fighter jets in international airspace, as the EurAsian Times has [noted](https://www.eurasiantimes.com/laser-weapons-china-fires-military-grade-dazzlers-at-p-8-poseidon-aircraft/) in the past.

However, US officials have repeatedly noted that China also has an inventory of ground-based laser weapons that could threaten satellites.

“Aside from missiles, the PLA has fielded multiple ground-based laser weapons able to disrupt, degrade, or damage satellite sensors. By the mid-to-late 2020s, we expect them to deploy systems high enough in power that they can physically damage satellite structures,” Gen. Chance Saltzman, Chief of US Space Operations, warned in a strongly worded statement last year.

China allegedly operates lasers capable of reversible effects, such as temporarily blinding satellites’ optical sensors in low Earth orbit, although more powerful configurations could permanently damage satellite sensors and other onboard components.

These systems, however, face operational limits from atmospheric distortion, line-of-sight constraints, weather, and the time required to slew and track targets.

Thus, putting lasers or microwaves in space would virtually remove these restrictions and provide unbridled access to potential targets. A satellite-based DEW could maintain longer dwell times on targets, engage satellites in higher orbits that are currently harder to reach from the ground, and potentially hold multiple targets at risk across successive orbits.

China currently has multiple anti-satellite weapons in space that could endanger US satellites providing critical communications and situational awareness to its troops on Earth during a conflict. However, deploying DEWs in space would let Beijing attack designated targets without the lasting orbital debris generated by kinetic anti-satellite missiles.

Notably, kinetic interceptors create debris that threatens everyone’s satellites for decades, while directed energy weapons are expected to leave the orbital environment largely intact. Therefore, these non-kinetic options offer clearer escalation control and reduced risk of self-inflicted damage, while allowing military planning to operate in a contested space domain and preserve access.

This could be bad news for the United States because a conflict with China is never off the table, especially in the event of a Taiwan invasion.

Currently, the US military operations depend heavily on space for navigation, ISR (intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance), missile warning, and communications.

Buy Home Safes

A capable orbital DEW capability would give China additional options to blind or degrade US or allied sensors and communications during a confrontation, especially in a Taiwan invasion scenario.

More importantly, it would give Beijing the option to conduct lower-escalation or deniable attacks targeting both LEO proliferated constellations (such as Starlink) and higher-orbit assets simultaneously. This would, in turn, complicate US space domain awareness, attribution, and response timelines.

At the same time, however, directed energy weapons could be employed defensively—to protect one’s own satellites from interference or attack—and to support space domain awareness and integrated defense architectures.

Legally, China is allowed to place DEWs or other conventional weapons in space because the 1967 Outer Space Treaty only prohibits the placement of nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit.

However, just because it can does not mean China can deploy or sustain directed energy weapons in space. This is because factors such as power generation, thermal management, beam control, and delivering militarily useful energy levels from a satellite remain substantial engineering challenges to fielding DEWs in space.

Whether China has overcome these obstacles sufficiently to field operational systems by the late 2020s remains to be seen.

title: Taiwan looks to autonomous swarms to counter Beijing’s grey-zone pressure
zh_title: 台湾寻求自主集群来对抗北京的灰色地带压力
summary: 据台湾海洋事务委员会称，台湾正在开发一种人工智能驱动的系统，以协调无人机机队进行海上监视和打击“灰色地带”活动，研究人员完成了涉及 20 架飞机的模拟。该系统由该委员会资助，将允许不同类型的无人机自主分配任务、规划路线并协调其行动，同时为海岸警卫队提供广域、持续的监视
content:
据台湾海洋事务委员会称，台湾正在开发一种人工智能驱动的系统，以协调无人机机队进行海上监视和打击“灰色地带”活动，研究人员完成了涉及 20 架飞机的模拟。

该系统由该委员会资助，将允许不同类型的无人机自主分配任务、规划路线并协调其行动，同时为海岸警卫队行动提供广域、持续的监视。

该委员会周一表示，由台湾国立成功大学领导的一个研究小组已经完成了由 20 架无人机组成的两个机队的同步飞行模拟，标志着从控制单架飞机到协调多个小组的转变。

解放军在台湾周边举行军事演习

该早期项目重点关注三款美国制造的垂直起降（VTOL）固定翼无人机——JUMP 20、V-BAT和Flexrotor——并集成了人工智能（AI）、飞行动力学和群体控制技术。

研究人员正在使用基于人工智能的多智能体强化学习，使飞机能够自主分配任务、规划路线并相互协调。
该项目还结合了主从编队控制和动态避障功能，使无人机能够根据不断变化的任务、条件和障碍物调整路线。

为了防止模拟中发生碰撞，研究人员将三维分离和飞机之间 30 米（100 英尺）的最小垂直距离编程到控制算法中。

该委员会表示：“下一阶段将涉及硬件在环测试、原型集成和在实际海域的飞行试验，以评估不同海洋和天气条件下的可靠性。”

报告表示，加强“海域意识”和发展空中和海上综合[海岸警卫队行动](https://www.scmp.com/news/china/military/article/3368380/taiwan-coastguards-rare-missile-firing-reveals-deepening-links-navy?module=inline&pgtype=article)对于日益增长的执法需求至关重要。

报告称，无人驾驶飞机可以提供“多无人机协调、广域覆盖和持续监视”，并在来自北京的“各种形式的灰色地带骚扰”中成为海岸警卫队人员的额外“天空之眼”。

北京将台湾视为中国的一部分，必要时可以用武力统一台湾。包括美国在内的大多数国家都不承认台湾是一个独立国家，但华盛顿反对任何以武力夺取这个自治岛屿的企图，并致力于向其提供武器。
这项研究是在台湾海岸警卫队扩大其无人驾驶飞机机队和接受操作此类系统培训的人员数量之际宣布的。

V-BAT 是美国国防技术公司 Shield AI 开发的一款尾座垂直起降无人机，可以在有限空间内运行，是正在推出的更先进的平台之一。

其涵道风扇设计使其能够从船上相对较小的区域起飞，然后过渡到水平飞行，而其超过 12 小时的续航时间可以实现长时间的海上监视。

两周前，海洋事务委员会公开公布了第一艘交付台湾的 V-BAT，主要用于训练。

【原文 English Original】
[Taiwan](https://www.scmp.com/topics/taiwan?module=inline&pgtype=article) is developing an AI-powered system to coordinate drone fleets for maritime surveillance and countering “grey-zone” activities, with researchers completing a simulation involving 20 aircraft, according to the island’s Ocean Affairs Council.

The system, which is funded by the council, would allow different types of [drones](https://www.scmp.com/topics/drones?module=inline&pgtype=article) to autonomously divide tasks, plan routes and coordinate their movements while providing wide-area, persistent surveillance for coastguard operations.

The council said on Monday that a research team led by Taiwan’s National Cheng Kung University had completed simultaneous flight simulations involving two fleets comprising 20 drones, marking a shift from controlling individual aircraft to coordinating multiple groups.

PLA kicks off military exercises around Taiwan

The early-stage project focuses on three US-made vertical take-off and landing (VTOL) fixed-wing drones – the JUMP 20, V-BAT and Flexrotor – and integrates artificial intelligence (AI), flight dynamics and swarm-control technologies.

Researchers are using AI-based multi-agent reinforcement learning to enable the aircraft to autonomously allocate missions, plan routes and coordinate with each other.

The project also incorporates leader-follower formation control and dynamic obstacle avoidance, allowing the drones to adjust routes in response to changing missions, conditions and obstacles.

To prevent collisions in the simulation, the researchers programmed three-dimensional separation and a minimum vertical distance of 30 metres (100 feet) between aircraft into the control algorithms.

“The next stage will involve hardware-in-the-loop testing, prototype integration and flight trials over actual maritime areas to assess reliability under different sea and weather conditions,” the council said.

It said strengthening “maritime domain awareness” and developing integrated aerial and maritime [coastguard operations](https://www.scmp.com/news/china/military/article/3368380/taiwan-coastguards-rare-missile-firing-reveals-deepening-links-navy?module=inline&pgtype=article) were central to growing law-enforcement needs.

Uncrewed aircraft could provide “multi-drone coordination, wide-area coverage and persistent surveillance” and be additional “eyes in the sky” for coastguard personnel amid “various forms of grey-zone harassment” from Beijing, it said.

Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

The research was announced as Taiwan’s coastguard expands both its uncrewed aircraft fleet and the number of personnel trained to operate such systems.

The V-BAT, a tail-sitter VTOL drone developed by US defence technology company Shield AI that can operate in confined spaces, is among the more advanced platforms being introduced.

Its ducted-fan design allows it to take off from a relatively small area on a ship before transitioning to horizontal flight, while its endurance of more than 12 hours allows prolonged maritime surveillance.

The first V-BAT delivered to Taiwan, which has been designated primarily for training, was publicly unveiled two weeks ago by Ocean Affairs Council Minister Kuan Bi-ling.

Taiwan’s Coast Guard Administration (CGA) has budgeted NT$1.2 billion (US$39 million) to acquire 12 V-BATs and six command-and-control systems, with the remainder of deliveries expected in the coming months.

Kuan said the introduction of sophisticated equipment must be accompanied by improvements in personnel skills and training, stressing that effective use of the technology was ultimately what mattered.

In July, the CGA took delivery of 45 multirotor training drones to distribute among coastguard units as part of a programme to familiarise frontline personnel with drone operation and eventually give officers basic operating skills, according to the administration.

02:55

Taiwan concludes annual war games, including preparing for PLA sea blockade

The broader programme is part of an Ocean Affairs Council initiative to develop what it calls an integrated “sea-air” coastguard, combining uncrewed platforms with upgraded intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance systems.

The council said recent conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East had shown how uncrewed aircraft were evolving from individually operated platforms towards coordinated fleets of different drone types.

For Taiwan’s coastguard, the shift could extend surveillance beyond the reach of ships and coastal sensors while allowing drones with varying capabilities to work together across a much wider area.

content:
_以下是2026年10月26日发布的日本2026年防卫白皮书的英文全文_

## 摘自报告

### 日本周边安全环境概要

**国际社会面临战后时代最大的考验**

不认同普世价值观或基于这种价值观的政治和经济制度的国家正在扩大其影响力。以武力单方面改变现状的企图是对现有国际秩序的严重挑战。国际社会正面临二战以来最大考验，进入危机新时代。全球力量平衡正在发生巨大变化，国家之间的竞争日益加剧。特别是，未来中美之间的国家间竞争可能会进一步加剧。

科学技术的快速发展正在从根本上改变安全范式。各国正在努力开发可以成为所谓游戏规则改变者的创新技术。传统的军事结构正在发生根本性变化，战争战术和战略也正在发生根本性变化。

网络空间等领域风险更加突出，信息战、气候变化等全球性安全问题不断涌现。
涉及领土争端的灰色地带局势不断发生。结合军事和非军事手段的混合战争的使用可能会变得更加复杂。
 印太地区安全形势日益严峻

这种全球安全环境和挑战在日本所在的印太地区尤为突出，并有可能进一步加剧。

不排除未来印太地区特别是东亚地区可能出现类似俄罗斯侵略乌克兰的严重局势。

**俄罗斯的侵略和乌克兰的防御**

俄罗斯对乌克兰的侵略损害了乌克兰的主权和领土完整。这严重违反了禁止使用武力的国际法和《联合国宪章》。这种单方面武力改变现状动摇了包括亚洲在内的国际秩序的基础。

一个本应对维护国际和平与安全负有首要责任的安理会常任理事国，公然从事挑战国际法和国际秩序的军事行动，夺走无辜生命，屡次使用可被解读为核武器威胁的语言和行动，这种情况是前所未有的。
如果容忍这种侵略行为，它可能会发出错误的信息，并暗示通过武力单方面改变现状在其他地方也是可以接受的。

因此，包括日本在内的国际社会不应容忍俄罗斯的行为。

除了乌克兰的强烈抵制外，国际社会还联合起来实施强有力的制裁等措施。作为美国的盟友（北约成员国）和横跨欧亚大陆与欧洲相对的国家，日本必须密切关注欧洲局势的未来变化，包括其战略影响，认识到欧洲和印太地区的安全密不可分。

【原文 English Original】
_The following is the full English translation of Japan’s 2026 Defense White Paper, released Oct. 26, 2026._

## From the Report

### Security Environment Surrounding Japan Overview

**International Community amid the Greatest Trial of the Postwar Era**

States that do not share universal values or political and economic systems based on such values are expanding their influence. Unilateral changes to the status quo by force and such attempts represent a serious challenge to the existing international order. The international community is facing its greatest trial since World War II and entering a new era of crisis. The global balance of power is shifting dramatically and competition among states is growing. In particular, the inter-state competition between the U.S. and China is likely to intensify even further in the future.

Rapid developments in science and technology are fundamentally changing the paradigm of security. Countries are striving to develop innovative technologies that can become so-called game changers. The traditional military structure is undergoing fundamental changes, as are warfare tactics and strategies.

Risks in cyberspace and other domains are becoming more serious, and other security-related global issues such as information warfare and climate change are emerging.

Gray zone situations involving territorial disputes are constantly occurring. The use of hybrid warfare, which combines military and non-military means, may become even more sophisticated.
 Increasingly Severe Security Situation in the Indo-Pacific Region

Such global security environment and challenges are particularly prominent in the Indo-Pacific region, where Japan is located, and are likely to intensify still further in the future.

It cannot be ruled out that a serious situation similar to Russia’s aggression against Ukraine may occur in the Indo-Pacific region in the future, particularly in East Asia.

**Russia’s Aggression and Ukraine’s Defense**

Russia’s aggression against Ukraine undermines the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine. It is a serious violation of international law prohibiting the use of force and of the United Nations (UN) Charter. Such unilateral changes to the status quo by force have shaken the very foundation of the international order, including in Asia.

This situation, in which a permanent member of the Security Council, which is supposed to take primary responsibility for maintaining international peace and security, openly engages in military actions challenging international law and the international order, claims innocent lives and repeatedly uses language and actions that can be interpreted as threats involving nuclear weapons, is unprecedented.

If such aggression is tolerated, it could send out the wrong message and implication that unilateral changes to the status quo by force are also acceptable elsewhere.

Accordingly, the international community, including Japan, should not tolerate Russia’s action.

In addition to Ukraine’s strong resistance, the international community has united to implement strong sanctions and other measures. As an ally of the U.S.—a NATO member—and a country located on the opposite side of Europe across the Eurasian continent, Japan must closely monitor future changes in the European situation, including their strategic impact, acknowledging that the security of Europe and the Indo-Pacific is inseparable.

**Defense Policies of Other Countries and Regions**

The U.S. – Security Policy and Activities of the Second Trump Administration

The second Trump administration was formed in January 2025. The National Security Strategy was released in December of the same year, followed by the National Defense Strategy in January 2026. These documents clarified the security strategy envisioned by the second Trump administration.

Under the banner of “America First,” the Department of War indicated its intention to restore “peace through strength” and to focus on the Indo-Pacific region, where Japan is located, while prioritizing homeland defense. The documents also provide detailed descriptions of relations with allies, among other matters.

**China – Intensified Unilateral Attempts and Activities to Change the Status Quo by Force or Coercion**

China’s external posture, military activities, and other activities are a matter of serious concern for Japan and the international community and present an unprecedented and the greatest strategic challenge which Japan should respond with its comprehensive national power and in cooperation and collaboration with its ally, like-minded countries, and others.

For more than 30 years, China has sustained high-level growth of its defense budget without transparency, engaging in broad and rapid improvement of its military power in qualitative and quantitative terms with a focus on nuclear, missile, naval, and air forces.

China has been intensifying its activities in the region surrounding Japan, including the East China Sea, particularly in the area around the Senkaku Islands, the Sea of Japan, and the western Pacific Ocean, extending beyond the so-called first island chain to the second island chain.

In 2025, a series of incidents occurred, including: the activity of an aircraft carrier in the waters east of Iwo-To and the activity of two aircraft carriers in the Pacific Ocean in June; the unusual close approach by a Chinese fighter aircraft to a Japan Self-Defense Forces (JSDF) aircraft in June; the unusual close approach by a Chinese fighter-bomber to a JSDF aircraft in July; the activity of an aircraft carrier in the Pacific Ocean from the east of the main island of Okinawa to the east of Amami Oshima Island in December; and intermittent radar illumination against a JSDF aircraft by a Chinese fighter for approximately 30 minutes in December.

Such unusual close approaches by Chinese military aircraft could have triggered an accidental collision. Furthermore, the radar illumination by the Chinese military aircraft was a dangerous act exceeding the range necessary for the safe flight of an aircraft, and it is extremely regrettable that such incidents took place.

China has intensified its military activities around Taiwan. China conducted military exercises in the sea and airspace several times. It is believed that through the series of activities, China seeks to create a fait accompli where the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) is operating, and improve its actual combat capabilities.

China has intensified its activities in the South China Sea, while promoting militarization, based on assertions of unlawful maritime claims. Such actions to further promote its attempts to unilaterally change the status quo by force or coercion are serious concerns to Japan. Issues surrounding the South China Sea are directly connected to peace and stability in the Indo-Pacific region and represent a legitimate concern, not only for Japan, which has major sea lanes in the South China Sea, but also for the entire international community.

China is further strengthening its cooperation with Russia, including in military activities. In the Commemoration of the 80th Anniversary of the Victory in the Chinese People’s War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War in September 2025, President Xi Jinping, President Vladimir Putin, and Chairman of the State Affairs Commission Kim Jong Un were seen standing side by side. In the vicinity of Japan, China and Russia conducted joint flights of bombers and joint navigations of vessels. Such repeated joint activities are obviously intended as demonstration activities against Japan and pose a grave concern for Japan’s security.

Taipei, Oct. 27 (CNA) Mayoral and magistrate candidates across Taiwan drew ballot numbers Tuesday for the Nov. 28 local elections.

Candidates are identified by number on Taiwanese ballots, and campaign teams build slogans around the number selected.

Draws took place at election commission venues across the country. Some candidates attended in person, while others sent representatives to draw numbers on their behalf.

Supporters cheered as the numbers were announced, and campaign teams quickly used the selected numbers in their campaign slogans.

The following are the results of the ballot-number lottery for the main contenders in Taiwan's six special municipalities:

## **Taipei**

Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋, center) draws No. 3 in a ballot-number lottery for the 2026 local elections in Taipei on Tuesday. Shen's team promoted the slogan "Taipei backs No. 3." CNA photo Oct. 27, 2026

Kuomintang (KMT) Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安, center) draws No. 5 as he seeks reelection in the 2026 local elections in Taipei on Tuesday. His team chanted "No. 5 Chiang Wan-an, Taipei, encore!" after the draw. CNA photo Oct. 27, 2026

## **New Taipei**

A representative draws No. 1 on behalf of DPP New Taipei mayoral candidate Su Chiao-hui (蘇巧慧) in a ballot-number lottery for the 2026 local elections in New Taipei on Tuesday. Su's campaign team celebrated with the slogan "In 2026, we will definitely win." CNA photo Oct. 27, 2026

A representative of KMT New Taipei mayoral candidate Lee Shu-chuan (李四川) draws No. 3 in a ballot-number lottery for the 2026 local elections in New Taipei on Tuesday. His team responded with the slogan "Vote No. 3, support Shu-chuan." CNA photo Oct. 27, 2026

## **Taoyuan**

KMT Taoyuan Mayor Chang San-cheng (張善政) draws No. 2 as he seeks reelection in the 2026 local elections in Taoyuan on Tuesday. Chang said the number symbolized "double good fortune" and expressed hope for continued public support. CNA photo Oct. 27, 2026

DPP Taoyuan mayoral candidate Huang Shih-chieh (黃世杰) draws No. 1 in a ballot-number lottery for the 2026 local elections in Taoyuan on Tuesday. Huang, known by the nickname "Penguin Dad," promoted the slogan "Penguins persevere, Taoyuan comes first." CNA photo Oct. 27, 2026

## **Taichung**

DPP Taichung mayoral candidate Ho Hsin-chun (何欣純, center) draws No. 1 in a ballot-number lottery for the 2026 local elections in Taichung on Tuesday. Supporters cheered with the slogan "For a good mayor, Taichung comes first." CNA photo Oct. 27, 2026

KMT Taichung mayoral candidate Johnny Chiang (江啟臣, third right) draws No. 3 in a ballot-number lottery for the 2026 local elections in Taichung on Tuesday. Chiang said the number symbolized his commitment to being a solid backer for Taichung residents. CNA photo Oct. 27, 2026

## **Tainan**

A city council candidate draws No. 2 on behalf of KMT Tainan mayoral candidate Hsieh Lung-chieh (謝龍介) in a ballot-number lottery for the 2026 local elections in Tainan on Tuesday. CNA photo Oct. 27, 2026

DPP Tainan mayoral candidate Chen Ting-fei (陳亭妃) draws No. 3 in a ballot-number lottery for the 2026 local elections in Tainan on Tuesday. Chen promoted the slogan "Tainan's first female mayor, backed by the people." CNA photo Oct. 27, 2026

## **Kaohsiung**

DPP Kaohsiung mayoral candidate Lai Jui-lung (賴瑞隆) draws No. 5 in a ballot-number lottery for the 2026 local elections in Kaohsiung on Tuesday. He shouted his campaign slogan in Taiwanese: "Kaohsiung's future belongs to you and me." CNA photo Oct. 27, 2026

KMT Kaohsiung mayoral candidate Ko Chih-en (柯志恩, center) holds up her No. 3 ballot number after the draw for the 2026 local elections in Kaohsiung on Tuesday. CNA photo Oct. 27, 2026

(By Lee Hsin-Yin)

title: 中共召开五中全会：“从严治党”背后的权力布局与政治刚需

content:
为期四天的中共二十届五中全会星期一(10月26日)在北京开幕。外界普遍认为这次闭门会议要为2027年召开的中共二十一大作准备。分析人士认为，本届全会聚焦“从严治党”是习近平的政治刚需；另外，会议可能只会对中共高层进行局部调整，而不会全面重新洗牌。

根据中国官媒报道，中共总书记习近平10月26日代表中央政治局向全会作工作报告，并就《中共中央关于持之以恒推进全面从严治党若干重大问题的决定(讨论稿）》向全会作了说明。

对于许多海外观察人士来说，虽然中共党内反腐行动、加强干部监督和问责等问题都是重要话题，但是全面从严治党才是五中全会的最主要议题。

人权组织“公民力量”(Citizen Power Initiatives for China)创办人杨建利告诉美国之音(VOA)，习近平上台十多年，权力已经非常集中，但是高调讨论“从严治党”仍是刚需。

**观察人士：对习来说，权力越集中越需要持续“从严治党”**

杨建利表示，对习近平来说，“从严治党”不光是反腐，也是巩固权力、统一思想、约束官僚体系的手段，权力越集中越需要持续做。

杨建利告诉美国之音，习近平多年清洗党内本身说明问题一直在冒出来，军队和要害部门接连出事，最高层很可能认为还没有清理干净。

杨建利说：“在二十一大之前，可以借这个机会把‘自我革命’的体系定型，作为执政遗产，也为人事布局铺路。”

杨建利认为，“从严治党”同时也是习近平本人的政治需要。他指出：“党内有人质疑‘反腐’，习近平要为自己的标志性政治路线，即反腐，盖棺论定，确定其正确性，避免翻案。”

《北京之春》杂志荣誉主编胡平甚至预测，习近平不仅要大张旗鼓讨论“从严治党”，而且还可能对这个问题做出一个相应的“决定”或者“决议”，因为反腐是习近平上台以来最主要的工作，他需要以中央全会的名义在反腐问题上给他一个正式的肯定。

胡平在接受美国之音采访时说：“他(习)知道反腐在内部造成了高度的紧张，有很多人对他的这些做法非常非常不满。因此他必须通过这么一个决定，把不同的声音给压下去。因此这是他在这次会上的重点。”

**美智库：出席五中全会的人数将降至毛泽东时代以来的最低水平**

美国亚洲协会政策研究所(ASPI)中国分析中心10月19日发布了一篇题为《习近平控制力的局限：中共五中全会观察重点》的文章，分析了中共二十届五中全会的核心议题、人事变动及政治走向。

文章开篇便称习近平“像是一位‘列宁主义版’的洛根·罗伊(Logan Roy）”。洛根·罗伊是美剧《继承之战》(Succession)中一位专横跋扈的大家长，他执掌着世界上最大的传媒娱乐集团之一，行使着绝对的权威，却又抱怨那些无法落实其想法的下属。

文章指出，习近平在党内开展的整肃行动，将导致五中全会会场出现许多空位。文章主要作者、“亚洲协会政策研究所”资深研究员牛犇(Neil Thomas)在社媒平台X上发帖指出：“据我们估算，出席此次全会的中央委员及候补委员人数，将降至毛泽东时代以来的最低水平，仅占总数的77%。”

对于外界关注的五中全会上是否会有更多的高官遭到清洗，长期观察和分析中国政治的杨建利表示，按惯例，全会上会确认此前已经查处的中央委员、候补委员的处分，并递补候补委员，名单很可能包括军队将领和部分省部级官员。

杨建利告诉美国之音：“全会当场宣布新的大老虎比较少见，更多是追认已经处理的人。但是全会后，清洗将会继续。”

《北京之春》荣誉主编胡平认为，党内清洗在五中全会开会前便已经结束，该处理的人员习近平已经处理好了。

胡平告诉美国之音：“(习)反而还可能把有些人补充上来，因为有的缺员太多了，他需要补充。”

**会不会有重大的权力布局？**

本届五中全会距离明年秋季召开的中共二十一大不到一年，外界普遍认为这是中共最高领导层换届前夕的重要政治节点，因此，权力布局和高层动向备受关注。

其中，中央军委人事变动特别是外界广泛关注的一个重点。在中共二十大产生的七人中央军事委员会中，包括李尚福、苗华、何卫东、张又侠和刘振立在内的五位成员，在习近平的军中反腐运动中先后落马，如今只剩习近平和张升民两人。

观察人士普遍认为，本届五中全会很有可能增补军委副主席或委员，而不会等到明年二十一大的召开。

不过，杨建利告诉美国之音，五中全会上大概率只是对高层进行局部调整，而不会是全面重新洗牌。

杨建利说：“补齐空缺的中央委员；很可能调整中央军委成员；政治局常委层面大幅变动的可能性较低。全会奠定基础，真正的重大布局在会后，包括可能的接班人选，更可能留到二十一大。”

杨建利强调说，本届全会的人事和措辞，均可“看作二十一大前的风向标”。

title: Hong Kong lawmakers’ monthly pay tops HK$110K after unannounced 1.6% salary rise
zh_title: 香港立法会议员未经宣布加薪1.6%，月薪突破11万港元
summary: 香港立法会议员在冻薪一年后获准加薪，追溯至10月1日，每月基本工资超过11万港元。即将离任和新当选的香港立法会议员于 2025 年 12 月 9 日与新闻界会面。照片：HKFP。 《星岛日报》周二上午报道称，立法会在其网站上更新了数字，但立法会议员已收到未经宣布的 1.6% 加薪。加薪后，议员的基本月薪将增加1,740港元至110,053港元。最高医疗津贴也将增加
content:
香港立法会议员在冻薪一年后获准加薪，追溯至10月1日，每月基本工资超过11万港元。即将离任和新当选的香港立法会议员于 2025 年 12 月 9 日与新闻界会面。照片：HKFP。 《星岛日报》周二上午报道称，立法会在其网站上更新了数字，但立法会议员已收到未经宣布的 1.6% 加薪。加薪后，议员的基本月薪将增加1,740港元至110,053港元。最高医疗津贴亦将增加1.6%至每年38,500港元。立法会主席李慧琼的底薪是其他议员的两倍，月底薪达221,060港元。立法会内务委员会主席陈振英的月薪是其他立法会议员基本月薪的1.5倍，加薪后每月收入为165,800港元。目前担任行政会议成员的议员，包括刘江明、吴季礼和陈家良，与其他立法会议员相比，收入较低。他们的每月基本工资将从72,530港元增加至73,690港元。 2012年，香港立法机关的席位从60个扩大到70个。2021年，北京彻底改革了立法机关的选举制度，将席位扩大到90个。大多数传统反对派人物仍被关在监狱中、离开政坛或自我流放。
2026 年 1 月 8 日，香港立法会议员李慧琼当选立法会主席后与其他议员握手。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。 10月初，1997年回归后香港立法会首任主席范丽泰在香港电台表示，维持立法会90名议员的成本太高，并援引“一位朋友”的意见。 《星岛日报》周二报道称，范的言论在政界引起广泛讨论，公众期望议员的表现能更好地“证明他们的薪酬合理”。今年早些时候，香港批准公务员、法官和司法官员加薪2%，最高部长和其他政治任命人员加薪1.3%。

【原文 English Original】
Hong Kong lawmakers have been given a pay rise retroactive to October 1 after a one-year pay freeze, bringing their monthly basic salary to more than HK$110,000. Outgoing and newly elected Hong Kong lawmakers meet the press on December 9, 2025. Photo: HKFP. Sing Tao Daily reported on Tuesday morning that legislators had received an unannounced 1.6 per cent pay rise, although the Legislative Council updated figures on its website . Following the pay rise, lawmakers will receive a basic monthly salary of HK$110,053, an increase of HK$1,740. The maximum medical allowance will also be increased by 1.6 per cent to HK$38,500 per year. The basic salary of Legislative Council President Starry Lee is double that of other lawmakers, bringing her basic monthly salary to HK$221,060. Chan Chun-ying, chairman of LegCo’s House Committee, receives 1.5 times the basic monthly salary of other lawmakers, earning HK$165,800 per month after the pay rise. Lawmakers who currently serve as members of the Executive Council, including Kenneth Lau, Stanley Ng and Gary Chan, earn less compared to other legislators. Their monthly basic salary will rise from HK$72,530 to HK$73,690. ‘Justify their pay’ Hong Kong’s legislature was expanded from 60 to 70 seats in 2012. In 2021, Beijing overhauled the electoral system for the legislature, expanding it to 90 seats. Most traditional opposition figures remain in prison, have left politics, or have fled into self-imposed exile. Hong Kong legislator Starry Lee shakes hands with other lawmakers after being elected as Legislative Council president on January 8, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Earlier in October, Rita Fan, the first president of Hong Kong’s legislature after the 1997 Handover, said on RTHK that it was costing too much to sustain 90 lawmakers in the Legislative Council, citing the opinions of “a friend.” Sing Tao Daily reported on Tuesday that Fan’s remarks were widely discussed in political circles, and the public expected lawmakers’ performance to better “justify their pay.” Earlier this year, Hong Kong approved a 2 per cent pay rise for civil servants, judges and judicial officers, and a 1.3 per cent pay rise for top ministers and other political appointees.

title: USAF should buy newly designed air refuelers to meet China threat: Report
zh_title: 美国空军应购买新设计的空中加油机以应对中国威胁：报告
summary: 华盛顿——一份智库报告称，美国空军需要大量投资来支撑其空中加油机队，从有针对性的基础设施支出到设计具有更大航程和燃油卸载能力的新型加油机。哈德逊研究所专家 Timothy Walton 和 Shane Dennin 今天发布的[报告](https://www.hudson.org/preview-link/node/52774/b3bee0ca-4908-4f47-9449-e711f8e19e0f) — 标题为_Resilient Reach：为有争议的全球运营重新设计空中加油_ — 提供了全面的观点空军的空中加油能力。目前该服务
content:
华盛顿——一份智库报告称，美国空军需要大量投资来支撑其空中加油机队，从有针对性的基础设施支出到设计具有更大航程和燃油卸载能力的新型加油机。

哈德逊研究所专家 Timothy Walton 和 Shane Dennin 今天发布的[报告](https://www.hudson.org/preview-link/node/52774/b3bee0ca-4908-4f47-9449-e711f8e19e0f) — 标题为_Resilient Reach：为有争议的全球运营重新设计空中加油_ — 提供了全面的观点空军的空中加油能力。报告称，该军种目前依赖“脆弱的前沿基地”和航程不足的加油机，增加了在与中国直接冲突中失败的风险。

在调查结果中，报告指出，波音制造的 [KC-46 Pegasus](https://breakingdefense.com/tag/kc-46/) — 正在慢慢取代空军艾森豪威尔时代的 [KC-135 Stratotanker](https://breakingdefense.com/tag/kc-135/) — “缺乏航程、卸载和生存能力”，无法在与北京的冲突中获胜。为了保持空军的空中加油优势，报告建议了未来加油机规划的三个关键步骤：
* 开发和部署具有更大航程和燃油容量的中型加油机，例如混合翼机身 (BWB) 飞机。报告称，假设一支由 510 架加油机组成的机队，购买 260 架 KC-46 和 250 架 BWB 加油机的研发、采购和维护成本估计为 3,976 亿美元，比仅购买相同数量的 Pegasus 飞机少了约 155 亿美元。
* 通过基础设施投资和改进防御措施以及采用更大的分布式燃料存储等措施来增强机场的弹性。作者估计这些措施累计成本可能约为 355 亿美元。
* 为加油机配备新的任务系统，以增强连通性、改善操作并帮助自卫。该报告估计这些升级可能花费大约 130 亿美元，其中包括装备 260 架 KC-46 机队所需的 80 亿美元。

军方官员称该平台在最近的“史诗狂怒”等作战行动中取得了成功，“空军有继续购买 KC-46 的诱惑，”沃尔顿在报告发布前接受《Breaking Defense》采访时表示。尽管如此，“显然需要一种超越 KC-46 提供的新方法。”
一位空军发言人告诉 Breaking Defense，该军种正在投资加油机容量、改进 KC-46 并开发下一代加油能力，同时寻求后续解决方案来解决机队生存能力。波音公司请空军发表评论。

空军去年公布了计划[额外订购 75 架 KC-46](https://breakingdefense.com/2025/10/how-a-priority-on-next-gen-tankers-paved-the-way-for-more-boeing-kc-46s/)，同时空军研究下一代加油机的选择。沃尔顿认为 75 架飞机“应该是购买的上限”，并认为空军应该优先开发一架新加油机。根据未来的预算限制，这种方法可能需要进行权衡，例如削减 KC-46 采购。

该报告概述了空军加油机机队的五种不同方法，从仅购买飞马座飞机到部署 KC-46、KC-135 和专门用于在靠近战斗的地方卸载燃料的不易察觉的专用加油机。虽然每种方法都有

【原文 English Original】
WASHINGTON — The US Air Force requires a slew of investments to shore up its air refueling fleet, from targeted infrastructure spending to designing a new tanker with greater range and fuel offload capacity, according to a think tank report.

Published today, the [report](https://www.hudson.org/preview-link/node/52774/b3bee0ca-4908-4f47-9449-e711f8e19e0f) by Hudson Institute experts Timothy Walton and Shane Dennin —titled _Resilient Reach: Redesigning Aerial Refueling for Contested Global Operations_ — offers a comprehensive view of the Air Force’s air refueling capacity. The service currently relies on “vulnerable forward bases” and tankers with insufficient range,increasing the risk of defeat in a direct conflict with China, the report says.

Among its findings, the report notes that the Boeing-built [KC-46 Pegasus](https://breakingdefense.com/tag/kc-46/) — which is slowly replacing the Air Force’s Eisenhower-era [KC-135 Stratotanker](https://breakingdefense.com/tag/kc-135/) — “lacks the range, offload and survivability” to prevail in a conflict with Beijing. To retain the Air Force’s aerial refueling advantage, the report recommends three key steps for future tanker planning:

*   Develop and field a medium-sized tanker with greater range and fuel capacity, such as a blended-wing body (BWB) aircraft.Assuming a fleet of 510 tankers, acquiring 260 KC-46s and 250 BWB refuelers could cost an estimated $397.6 billion across R&D, procurement and sustainment — about $15.5 billion less than simply buying only the same number of Pegasus aircraft, according to the report.
*   Strengthen airfield resilience with infrastructure investments and improved defenses, along with steps like adopting greater distributed fuel storage. The authors estimate these measures could cumulatively cost approximately $35.5 billion.
*   Equip tankers with new mission systems to boost connectivity, improve operations and aid self-defense. The report estimates these upgrades could cost roughly $13 billion, including $8 billion necessary to outfit a fleet of 260 KC-46s.

Following what military officials have described as the platform’s success in recent combat operations like Epic Fury, “[t]here’s a temptation for the Air Force to continue buying KC-46s,” Walton told Breaking Defense in an interview ahead of the report’s release. Still, “there’s clearly a need for a new approach that goes beyond what the KC-46 provides.”

An Air Force spokesperson told Breaking Defense that the service is investing in tanker capacity, improving the KC-46 and developing next-generation refueling capabilities while pursuing follow-on solutions to address fleet survivability. Boeing deferred to the Air Force for comment.

The Air Force last year unveiled plans to [order up to 75 additional KC-46s](https://breakingdefense.com/2025/10/how-a-priority-on-next-gen-tankers-paved-the-way-for-more-boeing-kc-46s/) while the service studies options for a next-gen tanker. Walton reasoned that 75 aircraft “should be the upper limit of that buy” and argued that the service should prioritize developing a new tanker. Depending on future budget constraints, that approach could require trade-offs such as trimming KC-46 procurement.

The report outlines five different approaches to the Air Force’s tanker fleet, ranging from purchasing only Pegasus aircraft to fielding a mix of KC-46s, KC-135s and specialized, low-observable refuelers designed to offload fuel closer to the fight. Though each approach has its own strengths, Walton highlighted fielding a medium-sized BWB aircraft as a desirable and “fiscally achievable plan” — adding that such an aircraft could enter service around 2032.

The Air Force is [funding a BWB demonstrator aircraft](https://breakingdefense.com/2023/08/air-force-picks-startup-jetzero-to-build-blended-wing-body-demonstrator/) designed by startup JetZero, which military officials have described as a potential candidate for future mobility missions. Walton said the report used a “representative” BWB model, and that while JetZero’s aircraft may fit the bill, other vendors could offer viable designs.

**_RELATED:_**[**_Natilus secures Air Force contract to develop blended wing body aircraft_**](https://breakingdefense.com/2026/10/natilus-secures-air-force-contract-to-develop-blended-wing-body-aircraft/)

Iranian strikes that have [destroyed US aircraft on the ground](https://breakingdefense.com/2026/04/air-force-strategy-to-protect-aircraft-was-designed-for-china-will-it-work-for-iran/) also underscore the need for more resilient base infrastructure, including hardened fuel storage and aircraft shelters, Walton said.Top military brass have championed passive and active defenses at airfields, but not everyone agrees with measures to build more hardened aircraft shelters, including [Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Ken Wilsbach](https://breakingdefense.com/2026/07/usaf-chief-wilsbach-on-lessons-from-iran-t-7-flight-and-f-35-delays/).

“It’s probably most contentious to assert that tanker aircraft should also be under consideration for hardened aircraft shelters, or at least hangars that can cover them from observation,” Walton said. “But I think in light of what we’ve seen from Operation Epic Fury, it’s necessary.”

Walton argued that the Air Force could fund more resilient infrastructure through existing plans to increase spending on facilities, especially if those funding levels are sustained. As large aircraft that serve a critical need, refueling assets are often seen as high-priority targets, though Walton noted that hardened shelters have generally been built for fighters.

“It’s not necessarily more money, but it’s prioritizing the amount of money in the out-years,” he said.

The Air Force is incrementally equipping its mobility aircraft with modern communications equipment and [exploring self-defense systems](https://www.airandspaceforces.com/lawmakers-air-force-tankers-self-defense-move-fast/?_gl=1*7qsw3x*_up*MQ..*_ga*MTAzNzYzMzc2Ni4xNzkzMDYwMzY4*_ga_6ZPT8CC738*czE3OTMwNjAzNjgkbzEkZzAkdDE3OTMwNjAzNjgkajYwJGwwJGgxNTA0NTI5ODA2) that could defeat enemy attacks. But the service has [previously failed](https://www.defenseone.com/defense-systems/2024/07/air-force-wont-hit-target-connecting-its-mobility-fleet-commander-says/398312/) to meet ambitious targets for fleet connectivity, and Walton acknowledged that limited resources could constrain the report’s recommendations for new mission systems, including communications, self-defense and autonomy technologies.

“Moving forward, the Air Force will have to weigh its available budget to spend” on new mission systems alongside competing priorities, he said, like resilient infrastructure and fielding a clean-sheet tanker. “And that might lead to some hard decisions.”
